source_text:
Homilia ii de Hypapante (homilia 2)
Ησυχίου, πρεσβυτέρου Ἱεροσολύμων, λόγος εἰς τὴν ὑπαπαντὴν τοῦ
κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.
1 Μὴ ἀγνοεῖτε ὅτι τὸ Πνεῦμα προφήτην τὸν Συμεῶνα κατέστη σεν καὶ
χρηματισμὸν αὐτῷ «μὴ ἰδεῖν θάνατον πρὶν ἰδεῖν τὸν Χριστὸν» προσεφώνησεν; «Νῦν
ἀπολύεις τὸν δοῦλόν σου, δέσποτα, κατὰ τὸ ῥῆμά σου ἐν εἰρήνῃ.» Οὐχὶ παρ' αὐτοῦ
χορηγηθεὶς τὸν Ἰωσὴφ καὶ Μαριὰμ εὐλόγησεν; Οὐ παρ' αὐτοῦ προσταχθεὶς τῇ
Μαριὰμ προσεφώνησεν· «Ἰδοὺ οὗτος κεῖται εἰς πτῶσιν καὶ ἀνάστασιν πολλῶν ἐν τῷ
Ἰσραήλ»; Οὐ δι' αὐτοῦ κάτοχος ἡ Ἅννα ὡς προφῆτις ἐτύγχανεν; Οὐκ ἐξ αὐτοῦ
μεστωθεῖσα τὴν ἐσομένην λύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ βρέφους κατήγγειλεν;
2 Τούτων ὑμῖν ἔδει κατὰ μέρος ὑφᾶναι τὴν ἐξήγησιν, ἀλλ' ἴσως ὁ καιρὸς
δεδαπάνηται καὶ τὸν λόγον ἐπιτεμεῖν φειδοῖ τῆς ὑπακοῆς τῆς ὑμετέρας προσῆκεν. Εἰ
δὲ οὐκ ἀνεκτὸν ὑμῖν τὸ ῥῆμα ἐπειδὴ συμποσιασταὶ τῆς τραπέζης ἐστὲ τῶν λογίων
τῶν ἱερῶν ἀκόρεστοι, ὅθεν ὑμῖν ὁ τῶν εὐαγγελίων συγγραφεὺς τὴν ἱστορίαν
ἤρξατο, ἐκεῖθεν ὡς ἔνι καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιτεμεῖν τὴν ἑρμηνείαν προσῆκεν, ὥστε καὶ τῷ
καιρῷ γενέσθαι καὶ τῷ πόθῳ τῷ ὑμετέρῳ τὰ πρόσφορα.
3 «Καὶ ἰδοὺ ἄνθρωπος ἦν ἐν Ἰερουσαλὴμ ᾧ ὄνομα Συμεών.» Οὐ μικρὸν
ἐγκώμιον τὸ Πνεῦμα τούτῳ γε τῷ Συμεὼν ἐν προοιμίοις ὕφαινεν· «Ἰδοὺ γάρ, φησίν,
ἄνθρωπος ἦν ἐν Ἰερουσαλὴμ» ὃν πάλαι μὲν ἐζήτουν οἱ προφῆται καὶ ὁ νόμος ἐπόθει,
εὗρεν δὲ ἡ χάρις καὶ εὑροῦσα τοῖς ἑξῆς ἐστεφάνωσεν. Ὁ στέφανος πόθεν πλέκεται;
Πρόσεχε· «Καὶ ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὗτος δίκαιος καὶ εὐλαβής, προσδεχόμενος παράκλησιν
τῷ Ἰσραήλ.» Ζηλῶσαι τὸν Συ μεῶνα καὶ μακαρίσαι προσῆκεν ὅτι οὐ μόνον δίκαιος
ἦν ἀλλὰ καὶ εὐλαβὴς κακίας πάσης ἀπείχετο· ὡς δὲ «προσδεχόμενος παρά κλησιν τῷ
Ἰσραήλ», οὔτε περὶ τὰς ἀρετὰς κοπιῶν ἐνάρκα, οὐδὲ κακίας ἀπεχόμενος ἔκαμεν.
4 «Καὶ Πνεῦμα ἦν ἅγιον ἐπ' αὐτόν.» Θαυμαστὸν καὶ τοῦτο καὶ τοῖς
ἔμπροσθεν εἰρημένοις ἁρμόδιον· ναὸς γὰρ ὑπῆρχεν, κα θαρὸν εἶχεν τὸν νυμφῶνα
τῆς σαρκός, καὶ τῆς ψυχῆς ἡ παστὰς πάσης βιωτικῆς ἀράχνης ἐκαθάρευεν· ἐκεῖθεν
πρὸς ἑαυτὸν εἵλ κυσε τὴν κατοικίαν τοῦ Πνεύματος. «Καὶ ἦν αὐτῷ κεχρημα τισμένον
ὑπὸ τοῦ Πνεύματος τοῦ ἁγίου μὴ ἰδεῖν θάνατον πρὶν ἰδεῖν τὸν Χριστὸν κυρίου.»
Ὁρᾷς πηλίκον ἐστὶν εἶναι ναὸν θεοῦ· ἀπὸ ζωῆς εἰς ζωὴν οἱ τὸν βίον οὕτως
ἀσκηθέντες μετέρ χονται. Ὅθεν καὶ τῷ Συμεὼν «κεχρηματισμένον ἦν μὴ ἰδεῖν
θάνατον πρὶν ἰδεῖν τὸν Χριστὸν κυρίου», τουτέστι πρὶν ἴδῃ τὸν καταργοῦντα τὸν
θάνατον, πρὶν ἴδῃ τὸν τοὺς νεκροὺς ἐγείροντα, πρὶν ἴδῃ τὸν εἰς νυμφῶνα τοὺς
τάφους μεταβάλλοντα, πρὶν ἐκεῖνον θεάσηται ὅστις ἄφοβον αὐτῷ τὴν ἐντεῦθεν
ἀποδημίαν ἐρ γάζεται.
5 «Καὶ ἦλθεν ἐν τῷ Πνεύματι εἰς τὸ ἱερόν.» Οὐδὲ τοῦτο παρελθεῖν ἢ
παραδραμεῖν ἄξιον· ἀπόδειξις γὰρ ὅτι κατὰ πρόσταξιν τοῦ Πνεύματος τοῦ
ἐνοικοῦντος ἔπραττε καὶ οὔτε εἰς ἀγορὰς οὔτε τινὰς πράξεις χωρὶς αὐτοῦ ὅλως
ἐνέβαλλεν· ὅπου γε εἰς τὸ ἱερόν, οὐκ ἄλλως, ἀλλὰ γὰρ αὐτοῦ χειραγωγοῦντος
ἔρχεται. «Καὶ ἐν τῷ εἰσαγαγεῖν τοὺς γονεῖς τὸ παιδίον Ἰησοῦν τοῦ ποιῆσαι κατὰ τὸ
εἰθισμένον τῷ νόμῳ περὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐδέξατο αὐτὸν εἰς τὰς ἀγκάλας.» Τίνος
αὐτῷ τὸ βρέφος ὅπερ ἠγνόει μηνύσαντος; Ἀλ λὰ γὰρ δῆλον τοῦ κατοικοῦντος ἐν
αὐτῷ καὶ χρηματίζοντος Πνεύματος καὶ πάντως που πρὸς τὸν Συμεῶνα λέγοντος·
«∆ράμε, πρεσβῦτα, δράμε, σπεῦδε ἤδη, τάχος τὴν εὐλογίαν ἅρπασον, πρὶν ὁ ἀστὴρ
thought_title: The Spirit made Simeon prophet and temple
orientation: Hesychius opens his homily on the Presentation by asking his hearers whether they recognize that the Holy Spirit made Simeon a prophet, blessed through him, and filled Anna to proclaim redemption.
pass_a_gloss: Hesychius, presbyter of Jerusalem, discourse on the Presentation of our Lord Jesus Christ. Do you not know that the Spirit made Simeon a prophet and addressed to him an oracle, 'not to see death before seeing the Christ'? 'Now you release your servant, Master, according to your word in peace.' Was it not furnished by him that he blessed Joseph and Mary? Was it not commanded by him that he addressed Mary: 'Behold, this one lies for the fall and rising of many in Israel'? Was it not through him that Anna, possessed, was a prophetess? Was it not filled from him that she proclaimed the coming redemption through the infant? It was necessary for you to weave the explanation of these things part by part, but perhaps the occasion has been spent and it is fitting to cut short the discourse out of regard for your obedience. But if the word is not bearable to you, since you are fellow-banqueters of the sacred oracles, insatiable at the table, from where the writer of the gospels began the history for you, from there it is fitting for us also, as far as possible, to cut short the interpretation, so that both the occasion and your longing receive what is suitable. 'And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon.' Not a small encomium was the Spirit weaving for this Simeon in the prologue; 'For behold,' it says, 'there was a man in Jerusalem' whom long ago the prophets sought and the law desired, but grace found him and having found him crowned him with what follows. From where is the crown woven? Pay attention: 'And this man was righteous and devout, awaiting consolation for Israel.' It is fitting to envy Simeon and call him blessed because he was not only righteous but also devout, he kept away from all evil; and as 'awaiting consolation for Israel,' he neither grew numb while toiling at the virtues, nor did he grow weary while keeping away from evil. 'And the Holy Spirit was upon him.' This too is wondrous and fitting with what was said before; for he was a temple, he kept the bridal chamber of his flesh clean, and the bridal chamber of his soul was cleansing itself of every spiderweb of life; from there he drew to himself the dwelling of the Spirit. 'And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit not to see death before seeing the Christ of the Lord.' Do you see how great a thing it is to be a temple of God? From life to life those who have so trained their life pass over. Whence also to Simeon 'it had been revealed not to see death before seeing the Christ of the Lord,' that is, before he sees the one who abolishes death, before he sees the one who raises the dead, before he sees the one who changes tombs into bridal chambers, before he beholds that one who makes his departure from here fearless for him. 'And he came in the Spirit into the temple.' Not even this is worthy to pass by or run past; for it is a proof that he acted according to the command of the indwelling Spirit and neither into marketplaces nor into any affairs did he enter at all without him; since indeed into the temple, not otherwise, but with him leading by the hand he comes. 'And when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do according to what was customary in the law concerning him, he himself received him into his arms.' Who revealed to him the infant whom he did not know? But it is clear that it was the Spirit dwelling in him and giving oracles, and surely saying to Simeon: 'Run, old man, run, hasten now, quickly seize the blessing, before the star

The glossary requires 'consolation' for the consolation of Israel.
The glossary requires 'fall' and 'rising' for these terms.

pass_b_english: Do you not know that the Spirit made Simeon a prophet and announced to him as an oracle that he would not see death before seeing the Christ? “Now you are releasing your servant, Master, according to your word, in peace” (Luke 2:29). Was it not by the Spirit’s gift that he blessed Joseph and Mary? Was it not by the Spirit’s command that he spoke to Mary, “Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel” (Luke 2:34)? Was it not through the Spirit that Anna was possessed as a prophetess? Was it not from him that she, filled, proclaimed the redemption that was to come through the infant?

I should have woven the explanation of these things for you point by point, but perhaps the time has been spent, and it is fitting to cut the discourse short out of regard for your obedience. But if this proposal is unbearable to you, since you are fellow guests at the table of the sacred sayings and insatiable, then from the point where the Gospel writer began the story for you, from there it is fitting for us also to cut short the interpretation as far as possible, so that what is offered may suit both the occasion and your longing.

“And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon” (Luke 2:25). The Spirit was weaving no small praise for this Simeon in the opening words. “For behold,” it says, “there was a man in Jerusalem” whom the prophets had long sought and the law had desired, and grace found him and, having found him, crowned him with what follows. From where is the crown woven? Pay attention: “And this man was righteous and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel” (Luke 2:25). It is fitting to envy Simeon and call him blessed, because he was not only righteous but also devout, and he kept away from every evil. And as one “awaiting the consolation of Israel,” he did not grow numb while toiling for the virtues, nor did he grow weary while keeping away from evil.

“And the Holy Spirit was upon him” (Luke 2:25). This too is wonderful and fitting with what has been said before. For he was a temple; he kept the bridal chamber of his flesh clean, and the bridal chamber of his soul was pure of every spiderweb of worldly life. From there he drew to himself the dwelling of the Spirit. “And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before seeing the Christ of the Lord” (Luke 2:26). Do you see how great a thing it is to be a temple of God? Those who have trained their life in this way pass from life to life. For this reason it had been revealed to Simeon that he would not see death before seeing the Christ of the Lord—that is, before seeing the one who abolishes death, before seeing the one who raises the dead, before seeing the one who turns tombs into bridal chambers, before beholding the one who makes his departure from here fearless.

“And he came in the Spirit into the temple” (Luke 2:27). This too is not worthy to be passed over or run past. For it is proof that he acted according to the command of the indwelling Spirit, and he did not go into marketplaces or any affairs at all without the Spirit. Indeed, he comes into the temple in no other way than with the Spirit leading him by the hand. “And when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he also received him into his arms” (Luke 2:27–28). Who revealed the infant to him, whom he did not know? It is clear that it was the Spirit dwelling in him and giving him oracles, and surely saying to Simeon: “Run, old man, run; hurry now; quickly seize the blessing, before the star—

problems.quote: Was it not filled from the Spirit that she proclaimed
problems.source_quote: Οὐκ ἐξ αὐτοῦ μεστωθεῖσα τὴν ἐσομένην λύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ βρέφους κατήγγειλεν;
problems.why: ἐξ αὐτοῦ refers to the Spirit (αὐτοῦ = τοῦ Πνεύματος), not 'from the Spirit' as source of filling. The Greek asks 'Was it not from him [the Spirit] that she, having been filled, proclaimed...' The English 'filled from the Spirit' is awkward and potentially misreads ἐξ as source of filling rather than agent: she was filled by the Spirit, then proclaimed. Better: 'Was it not from him that she, filled, proclaimed...'
problems.fix: Was it not from him that she, filled, proclaimed the coming redemption through the infant?

problems.quote: if the word is not enough for you
problems.source_quote: Εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἀνεκτὸν ὑμῖν τὸ ῥῆμα
problems.why: οὐκ ἀνεκτὸν means 'not bearable/endurable,' not 'not enough.' The preacher says 'if the discourse is unbearable to you'—ironic, meaning 'if you can't stand to stop' or 'if my stopping is intolerable.' The English 'not enough' loses the irony and changes the sense: it's not about quantity but about their inability to endure ending.
problems.fix: But if the discourse is unbearable to you
problems.ruling: οὐκ ἀνεκτὸν = 'not bearable/endurable'; 'not enough' changes meaning from inability to endure stopping to insufficient quantity.

fixed: Corrected 'filled from the Spirit' to 'from him that she, filled' because ἐξ αὐτοῦ refers to the Spirit as the agent/source of the proclamation, not the source of filling; she was filled by the Spirit and then proclaimed.
Corrected 'not enough' to 'unbearable' because οὐκ ἀνεκτὸν means 'not bearable/endurable,' not 'not enough.'

problems.fix: But if this proposal is unbearable to you

problems.quote: the bridal chamber of his soul was cleansing itself of every spiderweb of worldly life.
problems.source_quote: καὶ τῆς ψυχῆς ἡ παστὰς πάσης βιωτικῆς ἀράχνης ἐκαθάρευεν
problems.why: ἐκαθάρευεν (from καθαρεύω) means 'was pure/free from,' not 'was cleansing itself of' (which confuses it with καθαρίζω), changing a state of purity into an ongoing process.
problems.fix: the bridal chamber of his soul was pure of every spiderweb of worldly life.
problems.ruling: ἐκαθάρευεν (καθαρεύω) means was pure/free from, not was cleansing itself (καθαρίζω); state turned into process.

ἐκαθάρευεν (καθαρεύω): state 'was pure', not process 'was cleansing itself', fixed to 'was pure of'.

last_rejected.quote: and he kept away from every evil. And as one
last_rejected.why: Source says 'every evil'; English drops 'every' (πᾶσης), weakening the claim.
last_rejected.fix: and he kept away from every evil
last_rejected.ruling: English 'every evil' renders πᾶσης; 'kept away from every evil' is present. No omission.

last_rejected.quote: he did not grow numb while toiling for the virtues, nor did he grow weary while keeping away from evil
last_rejected.source_quote: οὔτε περὶ τὰς ἀρετὰς κοπιῶν ἐνάρκα, οὐδὲ κακίας ἀπεχόμενος ἔκαμεν
last_rejected.why: Greek says he neither grew numb toiling for virtues NOR grew weary keeping from evil; English 'did not...nor did he' misplaces negation, suggesting he did both without negative effects rather than he did neither.
last_rejected.fix: neither did he grow numb toiling for virtues, nor did he grow weary keeping away from evil
last_rejected.ruling: 'did not...nor did he' correctly renders οὔτε...οὐδέ. Both verbs are negated; no negation error.

last_rejected.quote: the bridal chamber of his soul was cleansing itself
last_rejected.source_quote: τῆς ψυχῆς ἡ παστὰς πάσης βιωτικῆς ἀράχνης ἐκαθάρευεν
last_rejected.why: Greek is passive or middle 'was cleansed,' not reflexive 'cleansing itself'; soul is object of cleansing, not agent.
last_rejected.fix: the bridal chamber of his soul was cleansed of every spiderweb of worldly life
last_rejected.ruling: ἐκαθάρευεν is middle/passive; 'cleansing itself' is a valid middle sense. Not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: The Spirit was weaving no small praise for this Simeon in the opening words. "For behold," it says, "there was a man in Jerusalem"
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐ μικρὸν ἐγκώμιον τὸ Πνεῦμα τούτῳ γε τῷ Συμεὼν ἐν προοιμίοις ὕφαινεν· «Ἰδοὺ γάρ, φησίν, ἄνθρωπος ἦν ἐν Ἰερουσαλήμ»
last_rejected.why: Greek 'φησίν' attributes quotation to the Spirit (neuter subject), but English 'it says' obscures this; the Spirit speaks through the Gospel words.
last_rejected.fix: The Spirit was weaving no small praise for this Simeon in the opening words. "For behold," the Spirit says, "there was a man in Jerusalem"
last_rejected.ruling: 'it says' correctly renders φησίν with Πνεῦμα as subject. No obscurity; meaning preserved.
